how-much-occupancy-tax-will-i-have-to-se.text:
← STR Occupancy Tax Calculator

How much occupancy tax will you have to self-file this year?

A platform's payout summary and 1099-K report what it paid you and what it remitted on your behalf -- not what's left over. Every figure below is the calculator's own worked example, run through its monthly rollup and held steady across a year, and checked against calc.mjs in this page's test file.

Run this on your own stay

The worked example, per stay

This calculator's own defaults: a $250 nightly rate, 4 nights, a $150 cleaning fee — a $1,150.00 taxable base — taxed at a 6% state layer the platform fully collects and a 5% county layer it does not. That's $126.50 in total tax per stay: the platform collects $69.00 of it, and $57.50 is left for the host to track and remit directly.

The monthly rollup turns it into a real number

One $57.50 gap per stay is easy to shrug off. The calculator's monthly rollup multiplies it by the bookings-per-month figure you supply -- 6 in the worked example — and the gap stops looking small: $345.00 a month is not covered by the platform's own tax remittance, on top of the $414.00 a month it does collect.

Held steady across a year

Twelve months at that same pace is the annual planning total: multiply each monthly figure by 12.

FigurePer stayPer month (×6)Per year (×12 months)
Total tax owed$126.50$759.00$9,108.00
Platform collects$69.00$414.00$4,968.00
Host must self-file$57.50$345.00$4,140.00

$4,140.00 a year is the county layer alone, from one listing at a steady 6-bookings-a-month pace. A host reading only the platform's own tax-collected total ($4,968.00 a year in this example) would budget for the wrong number -- the total tax owed across the year is $9,108.00, and just over half of it never touches the platform's remittance at all.

This is a planning total, not a filing figure

The annual number above assumes every month looks like the one you entered, which is the same assumption the calculator's own "illustrative rollup only" label next to Bookings per month already warns about. A seasonal host should run the calculator once per season at that season's own pace rather than annualizing a single busy or quiet month. And when an actual return is due, total the real county-layer tax off your own booking records for the filing period -- this page exists to answer "how much should I be setting aside," not to replace that record-by-record total.

Common questions

How much occupancy tax will I have to self-file this year?

Whatever your uncovered tax layers add up to across every stay, not just one. On this calculator's own worked example -- a $250/night, 4-night stay with a $150 cleaning fee at 6 bookings a month -- the host-must-remit share is $57.50 per stay and $345.00 a month. Held steady across a full year, that is $4,140.00 the host has to track and file directly, none of it withheld by the platform at checkout.

Why doesn't my 1099-K or payout summary already show this?

Because it reports what the platform paid out and, separately, what it remitted on your behalf -- it doesn't reconcile the two against what was actually owed on every stay. In the worked example, the platform's own tax summary shows $69.00 collected per stay for the state layer and calls that handled. It has no reason to surface the $57.50 county layer it never had a collection agreement for, so that figure exists nowhere in the platform's paperwork -- only in a calculation like this one.

If the platform's summary says tax was collected, am I covered?

Only for the layers that summary actually names. A platform's collection agreement is set per taxing authority, so “tax collected: yes” on a payout statement can mean the state layer alone. On the worked example, $69.00 of the $126.50 owed per stay is genuinely handled -- the remaining $57.50 is not covered by that same sentence, and a host who reads “collected” as “all of it” misses the county filing entirely.

My bookings aren't the same every month -- does the annual figure still work?

Only as a planning estimate, not a forecast. The calculator's monthly rollup is explicitly illustrative -- it multiplies one stay's tax by a flat bookings-per-month figure you supply, and a year at that same pace is twelve of that number. A host with a strong summer season and a quiet winter should run the calculator separately for each season's own booking pace rather than annualizing one month, since the flat multiplication assumes a steadiness most calendars don't have.

How often do I actually have to file and pay the host-remit amount?

That depends entirely on the taxing authority, and this calculator doesn't know it -- filing frequency (monthly, quarterly, or annual) is set by the specific county or city tax office, not by the platform or by this tool. What this page gives you is the total to expect over a year; the authority's own registration paperwork, from when you set up the account you file under, states how often a return is due.

Does this replace keeping records for an actual filing?

No. This is a planning total from one representative stay and a monthly average, useful for deciding how much cash to set aside -- it is not a substitute for totaling each stay's actual county-layer tax off your own booking records when a return is due. Use the per-stay calculator on every real booking if you need a number to file, not this page's annualized estimate.

No warranty. This free tool is not legal, tax, accounting, or financial advice, and it is not a filing. It makes no determination about which taxing authorities apply to a specific listing, what a platform's current collection agreements cover, or what you owe. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type, including the annualized planning total above. Verify every figure against each taxing authority's own guidance, the platform's tax pages for that specific address, and a qualified tax professional before you rely on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Free and open source. If it saves you from a surprise county tax bill, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

how-to-find-your-platforms-collection-ag.text:
← STR Occupancy Tax Calculator

How to find which occupancy tax layers your platform already collects

There is no single published list. A platform's collection agreements are negotiated one state, county, and city at a time, so answering "which of my layers does Airbnb or Vrbo already remit?" means checking a few specific places, in order — not searching for one page that names them all.

Four places to check, in order

  1. The platform's own tax help page, searched by state, then by county or city. Airbnb and Vrbo each publish a jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction tax page. Search it by the listing's exact state first; if a collection agreement exists at the county or city level, it is usually named there rather than on a general state summary.
  2. Your payout statement's own line items. Some hosts see occupancy tax withheld as a separate line on individual payouts. That is proof a layer is covered — but its absence is not proof no tax is owed; it may only mean the platform never had an agreement for that layer in the first place.
  3. The taxing authority directly. Call or email the county tax collector's office, or the city finance or revenue department, and ask whether they hold a voluntary collection agreement with the specific platform for short-term rentals. This is the authority the money is actually owed to, so their answer is the one that controls if it conflicts with what a platform's help page implies.
  4. Your state department of revenue, for the state-level layer specifically. State sales or transient-occupancy tax is the layer most platforms cover most consistently, but confirm rather than assume — a newer or smaller platform, or a listing booked partly off-platform, can leave even the state layer uncollected.

Why a payout statement showing nothing does not mean nothing is owed

A payout statement is a record of what the platform actually did, not a determination of what you owe. If a county has no collection agreement with the platform, that county's tax never appears as a withheld line — the same blank line as a county with no tax at all. The two look identical on the statement and are not identical in what you owe. Confirming the agreement's existence, per step 3 above, is the only way to tell them apart.

Re-check before each filing period, not once

Collection agreements are added throughout the year as platforms and authorities finish negotiating them, and a jurisdiction that was entirely your own filing in January can become platform-remitted mid-year for stays booked afterward. A rate or coverage figure confirmed last year, or even last quarter, is worth re-checking rather than reusing — especially in a jurisdiction that has recently changed its short-term rental rules.

Once you know each layer's status, split the tax on your own stay →

This calculator ships no rate table and makes no determination about which authorities apply to a specific listing on purpose — see the FAQ on the calculator itself. This page is about where to find that answer, not what it is for you.

Common questions

Where does a platform publish its occupancy tax collection agreements?

Nowhere as a single list. Airbnb and Vrbo each maintain a tax help page searchable by state, and inside that a county or city section if an agreement exists there — but there is no downloadable table of every covered jurisdiction, because the agreements themselves are negotiated one authority at a time and change without a portfolio-wide announcement.

Does my payout statement tell me what was withheld?

Sometimes, as a line item, but only for the layers the platform actually withheld — it says nothing about a layer it did not, which is the one that matters for a self-filing decision. A statement showing tax withheld on a stay is evidence that layer is covered; a statement showing none is not evidence that no tax is owed, only that the platform did not collect any.

What if the platform's help page and the tax authority disagree?

Treat the taxing authority as controlling, since the money is owed to them either way, and ask in writing so you have a record of the answer for that specific address. A platform's public help page is written for its whole user base and can lag a new agreement or drop a jurisdiction during a redesign; a county or city tax collector's office can confirm what applies to one address.

Do collection agreements change during the year?

Yes, and without notice to individual hosts. A platform can add a jurisdiction mid-year once a new agreement is signed, which means a layer that was entirely the host's own filing in January can become platform-remitted in July for stays booked afterward. Re-check before each filing period rather than relying on a figure from a prior year.

No warranty. This page is not legal, tax, accounting, or financial advice, and it is not a filing. It makes no determination about which taxing authorities apply to a specific listing or what a platform's current collection agreements cover. Verify every figure against each taxing authority's own guidance, the platform's tax pages for that specific address, and a qualified tax professional before you rely on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. This page makes no network requests and collects nothing.

      Common questions

      Does Airbnb or Vrbo already pay my occupancy tax for me?

      Sometimes, and rarely all of it. Airbnb and Vrbo each hold collection agreements with some taxing authorities and not others, and those agreements are set per state, county, and city — not per platform. A common pattern is a state sales tax the platform collects and remits automatically, sitting next to a county tourist-development tax it does not, because no agreement covers that county. On the worked example below, $126.50 in total occupancy tax, the platform collects the $69.00 state layer in full and none of the $57.50 county layer, leaving that $57.50 for the host to track and file directly.

      How do I know which tax layers a platform already collects?

      The platform’s own tax help pages, searched by the specific state, county, and city the listing sits in — not by the state alone, since collection agreements are set per authority and a state-level page will not mention a county that is not covered. Some hosts also see it on their payout statement as a line item withheld. When in doubt, ask the county or city tax collector’s office directly whether they have a voluntary collection agreement with the platform for short-term rentals; that office is the authority the money is owed to either way.

      What counts as the taxable base for occupancy tax?

      Most jurisdictions tax the full amount a guest pays for the right to occupy the space, which is usually the nightly rate times nights plus the cleaning fee — not the nightly rate alone. On the worked example, $250 a night for four nights plus a $150 cleaning fee makes a $1,150.00 taxable base, and every tax layer below is a percentage of that figure. A jurisdiction that does not tax the cleaning fee is the exception rather than the rule; check the specific authority’s own guidance and enter $0 there if so.

      What tax rates should I use?

      The ones published by each taxing authority the listing’s address sits inside — state department of revenue, county tax collector, city finance office, and any special district that levies one. This calculator ships no rate table on purpose: rates vary by every layer of jurisdiction, they change, and a table baked into a free tool would be stale in the one place that is expensive to be wrong — a filed remittance. Enter each authority’s current rate and the arithmetic is yours to check.

      What is the flat per-night fee for?

      Some cities and counties charge a fixed dollar amount per night on top of, or instead of, a percentage tax — a tourism assessment or a lodging fee that does not scale with the room rate. It is kept separate from the percentage layers because it is computed differently: nights times a flat rate, not a share of the taxable base. Leave it at zero if the listing’s jurisdiction does not charge one.

      Is any of this uploaded?

      No. There is no account and the page makes no network requests — it runs entirely in your browser. Your nightly rate, fees, tax layers, and the figures worked out from them are never sent anywhere and never appear in a usage count. The optional counter records only which features were used and the day, stored on your own device, and it switches itself off for browsers sending Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control.

      Can I save this stay or send it to someone else?

      Yes. Your tax layers and the other fields are saved to this browser automatically, so they are still here on your next visit. The copy-link button puts the same figures into the page’s own address after the #, which is never sent to a server or logged anywhere, so sending it to a co-host or bookkeeper uploads nothing.

      Is this tax advice, and does it file anything?

      No to both. It is arithmetic on figures you type, using rates you supply. It is not tax advice and it files nothing — it makes no determination about which authorities tax a specific listing, what a platform’s current collection agreements cover, or what you owe. Verify every figure against each taxing authority’s own guidance, your platform’s tax pages for that specific address, and a qualified tax professional before you rely on it.

vs-tracking-it-in-a-spreadsheet.html.text:
← STR Occupancy Tax Calculator

This calculator vs. tracking occupancy tax in a spreadsheet

Occupancy tax is arithmetic, and a spreadsheet can do arithmetic. What a hand-built sheet usually misses is not the rate math but which layer of it a platform's collection agreement actually covers.

Where a hand-built spreadsheet usually goes wrong

QuestionCommon spreadsheet shortcutWhat this calculator does
Tax owedOne blended rate cell, or one row per authority with only a rate column.Up to four named layers, each with its own rate, plus a flat per-night fee some jurisdictions charge separately.
Who already remitted itUsually not modeled at all — a layer entered at a rate looks the same whether or not the platform withholds it.A per-layer "platform collects" percentage, splitting every layer into what is already covered and what is left for the host.
The taxable baseOften just the nightly total, with the cleaning fee tracked separately and left out of the tax math.Nightly rate times nights plus the cleaning fee, since most jurisdictions tax both.
Does anything I type get uploaded anywhere?N/ANo. The calculation runs entirely in your browser; nothing you enter is sent to a server.

What the missing distinction costs, on the calculator's own worked example

The stay this calculator opens with is $250 a night for four nights plus a $150 cleaning fee, for a $1,150.00 taxable base. A 6% state sales tax layer and a 5% county tourist-development tax layer together owe $126.50. A spreadsheet tracking only that blended 11% total shows the same figure and stops there.

The platform's collection agreement covers the state layer in full — $69.00 — and none of the county layer. That leaves $57.50 that never appears on a payout statement and is not withheld anywhere. A host reading only the blended total has no way to see that gap; a host reading a per-layer split sees exactly which $57.50 is theirs to file, on every stay, all year.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Open the STR Occupancy Tax Calculator to work your own stay, or compare payout fees across platforms with the STR host payout calculator.

Common questions

Isn't occupancy tax just a total rate I can put in a spreadsheet?

The arithmetic is simple — a percentage of a taxable base — and a spreadsheet handles that fine. What it does not do on its own is track each tax layer's remittance status separately: a state sales tax a platform collects automatically sitting next to a county tourist tax it does not. A single blended rate cell answers "what is owed" and stays silent on "who already paid it", which is the question that actually determines whether a host has a filing to do.

What does missing that distinction actually cost?

On the worked example this calculator opens with — a $1,150.00 taxable base, a 6% state layer the platform fully collects, and a 5% county layer it does not — the total tax is $126.50. A spreadsheet tracking only the blended 11% rate shows that figure and nothing else. The host still owes $57.50 in county tax with no reminder that it was never withheld, because the sheet never modeled the platform's collection agreement as a separate fact from the tax rate itself.

Why not just add a column for what the platform collects?

You can, and a correctly built sheet gets the same split this calculator does — it is the same arithmetic either way. What a spreadsheet will not do unprompted is flag the case worth flagging: a layer entered at a rate but never marked as either fully covered or fully uncovered, which looks in a cell exactly like a layer already handled. This calculator raises that flag on every stay; a spreadsheet only raises it if someone remembered to build the check.
